docs.text: MarkovBox Generatywny syntezator, który sam komponuje. MarkovBox to generatywny syntezator z wbudowanym sekwencerem opartym na łańcuchach Markowa. Większość syntezatorów gra tylko to, co zagra na nich człowiek. MarkovBox ma grać także wtedy, gdy człowiek tylko kręci gałkami: sekwencer wytrenowany na korpusie plików MIDI generuje melodie o regulowanej „przewidywalności”. Jedna gałka zmienia rząd modelu, druga temperaturę losowania, a instrument płynnie przechodzi od wiernego cytowania korpusu do kontrolowanego chaosu. Cel i zakres Celem projektu jest zaprojektowanie, zbudowanie i publiczne udostępnienie działającego zamkniętego w obudowie syntezatora generatywnego, wraz z pomiarową charakteryzacją toru audio i oceną odsłuchową generowanych sekwencji. Produkt obejmuje: silnik dźwięku: co najmniej synteza subtraktywna. sekwencer Markowa: parser MIDI, budowa macierzy przejść dla korpusu, sterowanie rzędem modelu i temperaturą. własne PCB i obudowę z druku 3D. publiczne repozytorium ze schematami, plikami PCB, firmware, obudowy i instrukcją złożenia. raport pomiarowy toru audio i nagrania demonstracyjne.

docs.text: Decision DEC-001: Selection of Embedded Microcontroller Platform Date: 25-10-2026 Area: Hardware Context We need an embedded microcontroller platform capable of running real-time audio synthesis. Key technical constraints: Memory: Sufficient RAM to hold large multi-order Markov transition tables in memory. DSP Performance: FPU support and enough clock speed for real-time audio synthesis. Development environment: Limited development time, requiring existing audio libraries rather than building from scratch. Options considered Option Pros Cons Daisy Seed - Mature libDaisy and DaisySP libraries - 64 MB SDRAM - High-performance ARM Cortex-M7 with hardware FPU - Built-in audio codec - Higher cost compared to basic microcontrollers - Currently out of stock (restock in November/December) RP2040 - Very low cost - Widely available - No FPU - Only 264 KB SRAM - Requires external I2S DAC Decision We choose Daisy Seed . Reasoning Daisy Seed provides us with the libDaisy and DaisySP libraries, which will drastically speed up our development process. It also offers significantly more RAM to store Markov transition tables, solving two of our biggest bottlenecks. The potential cost savings of choosing the RP2040 are not worth the heavy compromises its limited memory and lack of FPU would force on the way.

docs.text: Decision DEC-002: Selecting Synthesis Type for Our Sound Engine Date: 11-11-2026 Area: Sound Engine Related issue: #21 Related research: /research/fm_vs_subtractive_synthesis.md Context We need a synthesis engine for our synthesizer. The research compared the main synthesis types, focusing on FM vs subtractive. Key constraints: Sound variety: The engine should offer a broad range of timbres and room for experimentation. Complexity: Implementation effort must stay realistic for the project's timeframe. Hardware: The engine must run in real time on the Daisy Seed. Options considered Option Pros Cons Subtractive - Most common and well-known method - Simple signal chain - Lowest implementation complexity - Filter can only remove existing harmonics - Limited options for complex modulation and experimentation 4-op FM - Many operator connections - Wide variety of sounds, including inharmonic ones - Detailed control over the spectrum - Much higher implementation complexity - Many parameters to expose and tune - Less intuitive to program than a filter Decision We choose 4-operator FM synthesis , implemented as phase modulation: y(t) = A * sin(2*pi*fc*t + I * sin(2*pi*fm*t)) Reasoning Four operators connected in different algorithms give far more control over the spectrum and more room for experimentation than a basic subtractive synth. FM is clearly more complex to implement than subtractive synthesis, but we accept this on purpose. Digital FM is usually implemented as phase modulation, which is the approach we will follow.

docs.text: Decision DEC-003: Choosing a Method for Calculating Sine Values During Live Synthesis Date: 18-11-2026 Area: Sound Engine Related issue: #34 Context We need a fast way to calculate sine values during audio synthesis. Key constraints: Required power: We plan to implement 4-operator FM with four voices, which means 16 operators continuously evaluating the sine function. Options considered Option Pros Cons sinf() - Easy to use, no need to reinvent the wheel - 16 operators calling sinf() 48000 times per second would be computationally expensive Lookup table - Drastically reduces the computation time of an approximated sine - Less accurate approximation - Uses some memory, though not much Decision We choose the lookup table Reasoning A lookup table saves considerably more processing time than sinf() , and the memory it requires is minimal. The approximation is not as precise as sinf(), but a sufficiently large table combined with linear interpolation should be more than enough for our synthesis.

docs.text: Meeting MET-004: Sprint 2 Review Date: 19-11-2026 13:30-14:00 Form: online Members: Oktawian Bieszke, Mikołaj Domiński, Marcin Ptasiński, Oliver Tyszko, Szymon Zaporowski Goal Discuss tasks and goals reached. Question Discussed What should we focus on in our documentation, such as decisions taken? How thoroughly do we need to document everything, especially if we want to enter the dean’s competition? Any advice on whether there’s anything in particular we should focus on implementing to make our project stand out? Notes Progress report Focus on documenting as much as possible. Our project schedule has been approved. We will fill up our DTP/DPP with our GitHub docs later. Our synthesizer is going to implement polyphony. Markov chains: discussing polyphony or monophony due to the Daisy Seed's limited memory. Perhaps we'll add built-in effects for the synthesizer, or maybe sampling to make it even more sophisticated. Maybe add switching between synthesis types? Sound timbre settings are also possible to implement. Make this project and the documentation easily accessible so that users can easily build and flash their own models trained on their MIDI files. Meetings are confirmed to occur every other Thursday at 11:00. Budget for our BOM has been approved. Conclusions Discussed the current state of the project, and for now the work is going on smoothly. We are going to continue the creation of the FM sound engine and implement our Markov's model as well as focus even more on comprehensive documentation.
